---
title: "3. Validation"
subtitle: "The simulator, prior predictive checks and simulation-based calibration"
---


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
source("R/prepare-data.R")
source("R/priors.R")
source("R/simulate.R")
source("R/stan-data.R")
source("R/plot-theme.R")

lizards <- read_csv("data/lizards-spring-2024.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
design <- prepare_data(lizards)
n_prior <- 1000 # prior predictive draws
```
:::


Before the model is fitted to the real data, we check two things. First,
that the priors imply plausible lizards: plausible performance, survival
and resighting. Second, that the model recovers known parameter values
from data simulated with them. Both checks use a simulator that
generates data exactly as the model assumes they arise.

## The simulator

The simulator (`R/simulate.R`) mirrors the model in
[2. Model](02-model.qmd). It **conditions on the observed study
design**: every simulated dataset has the same
708 lizards, with their real species, sex, morphology, trial
temperatures and pattern of missing performance trials. Only the
quantities the model treats as random are simulated.

| Kept from the real data | Simulated |
|---|---|
| species and sex | the four performance traits |
| standardised morphology ($x_{ik}$) | survival to fall 2024 ($z_i$) |
| standardised trial temperatures ($w_{ij}$) | resighting in fall 2024 and spring 2025 ($y_{i2}, y_{i3}$) |
| which performance trials are missing | which leaf trials fall below the detection limit |
| the leaf detection limit on each species' scale ($c_s$) | |

### Workflow

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Simulator workflow. Functions are in `R/`. `simulate_one()` runs the whole chain and returns the true parameter values together with Stan-ready data."
flowchart LR
  D[data/lizards-spring-2024.csv] --> PD["prepare_data()"] --> DES[design]
  PR["priors (R/priors.R)"] --> DP["draw_params()"] --> PAR[true parameters]
  DES --> SD["simulate_data()"]
  PAR --> SD
  SD --> SIM[simulated data] --> MSD["make_stan_data()"] --> STAN[Stan data]
  PR --> MSD
```

The functions are:

1. **`prepare_data()`** turns the cleaned dataset into the model's
   inputs (the design) and the observed outcomes. The same function
   prepares the real data for fitting, so simulated and real data have
   identical structure.
2. **`draw_params()`** draws one set of parameters from the priors.
   - Species-level parameters are drawn from their across-species
     distributions, as in the model's hierarchy.
   - With `direct_effect = TRUE`, it also draws the direct effects
     $\gamma$ (model M2). Otherwise they are 0 (model M1).
3. **`simulate_data()`** generates outcomes for the design in four
   steps.
   - Performance vectors are drawn from their multivariate normal
     distributions, including the effect of trial temperature.
   - Survival is drawn from temperature-adjusted performance (and, in
     M2, morphology).
   - Resightings are drawn given survival.
   - The real missing-data pattern is applied, and leaf values below
     the detection limit are censored.
4. **`make_stan_data()`** adds the prior values and model flags,
   producing the data list for `stan/model.stan`.
5. **`simulate_one()`** runs steps 2--4 and returns the true parameter
   values (named as in Stan) along with the Stan data. This is the unit
   of simulation-based calibration.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2024)
example <- simulate_one(design, priors, direct_effect = TRUE)
```
:::


One call produces 197 true parameter values
under M2 (fewer under M1, which has no direct effects) and a complete
Stan data list.

### Self-consistency check

The simulator should generate data that reproduce the parameters used
to generate them. We test this with a design much larger than the real
one, so that estimates are precise. The design repeats the
*A. cristatellus* lizards 40 times (24,200
lizards), with every performance trait observed and no censoring. We
then fit the two submodels outside Stan:

- **Performance:** each trait is regressed on sex, size, its linked
  shape trait and trial temperature (linear and squared) by least squares.
- **Survival and detection:** the history likelihood from
  [2. Model](02-model.qmd) is maximised directly.

If the simulator and the likelihood agree, the estimates fall close to
the true values.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(3)
big <- design
rows <- rep(which(design$species == 2), 40)
for (nm in c("species", "male", "y2", "y3", "cens")) big[[nm]] <- design[[nm]][rows]
for (nm in c("x", "w", "u", "obs")) big[[nm]] <- design[[nm]][rows, , drop = FALSE]
big$N <- length(rows)
big$obs[] <- 1L
big$c_leaf[] <- -Inf

truth <- draw_params(big, priors, direct_effect = TRUE)
sim <- simulate_data(truth, big)
m <- big$male
x <- big$x

# performance: least squares per trait
perf_check <- map(seq_along(perf_traits), \(j) {
  X <- cbind(m, x[, "svl"], x[, big$shape[j]])
  true <- c(truth$alpha[2, j], truth$delta[2, j], truth$b_svl[2, j], truth$b_shape[2, j])
  names <- c("alpha", "delta", "b_svl", "b_shape")
  if (j <= ncol(big$w)) {
    X <- cbind(X, big$w[, j], big$w[, j]^2)
    true <- c(true, truth$t[2, j], truth$t2[2, j])
    names <- c(names, "t", "t2")
  }
  fit <- summary(lm(sim$u[, j] ~ X))$coefficients
  tibble(submodel = "performance", parameter = paste0(names, "[", perf_traits[j], "]"),
         true = true, estimate = fit[, 1], se = fit[, 2])
}) |>
  list_rbind()

# survival and detection: maximise the history likelihood
u_adj <- sim$u
u_adj[, 1:2] <- sim$u[, 1:2] - sweep(big$w, 2, truth$t[2, ], "*") - sweep(big$w^2, 2, truth$t2[2, ], "*")
negloglik <- function(th) {
  phi <- plogis(th[1] + th[2] * m + u_adj %*% th[3:6] + u_adj^2 %*% th[7:10] + x %*% th[11:15])
  p <- plogis(th[16] + th[17] * m)
  lambda <- plogis(th[18] + th[19] * m)
  y2 <- sim$y2
  y3 <- sim$y3
  prob <- case_when(
    y2 == 1 & y3 == 1 ~ phi * p * lambda,
    y2 == 0 & y3 == 1 ~ phi * (1 - p) * lambda,
    y2 == 1 & y3 == 0 ~ phi * p * (1 - lambda),
    TRUE ~ 1 - phi + phi * (1 - p) * (1 - lambda)
  )
  -sum(log(prob))
}
true_surv <- c(truth$a[2], truth$c[2], truth$beta[2, ], truth$q[2, ], truth$gamma[2, ],
               truth$pi[2], truth$zeta_p, truth$ell[2], truth$zeta_lambda)
opt <- optim(rep(0, length(true_surv)), negloglik, method = "BFGS",
             control = list(maxit = 2000), hessian = TRUE)
surv_check <- tibble(
  submodel = "survival & detection",
  parameter = c("a", "c", paste0("beta[", perf_traits, "]"), paste0("q[", perf_traits, "]"),
                paste0("gamma[", morph_traits, "]"), "pi", "zeta_p", "ell", "zeta_lambda"),
  true = true_surv, estimate = opt$par, se = sqrt(diag(solve(opt$hessian)))
)

check <- bind_rows(perf_check, surv_check) |>
  mutate(z = (estimate - true) / se)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
check |>
  mutate(parameter = fct_rev(fct_inorder(parameter))) |>
  ggplot(aes(z, parameter)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -2, xmax = 2, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "#ecebe8") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#b0afa9", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(colour = species_colours[["cris"]], size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-3.5, 3.5)) +
  facet_grid(submodel ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "(estimate − true) / SE", y = NULL) +
  theme_lizard() +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Self-consistency of the simulator for one large simulated dataset. Points are the standardised difference between estimate and true value, (estimate − true) / SE. If the simulator and the likelihood agree, these behave like standard normal draws: most within ±2 (shaded band).](03-validation_files/figure-html/fig-self-consistency-1.png){#fig-self-consistency width=768}
:::
:::


Of the 39 parameters, 36 are
within 2 standard errors of their true values, and the largest deviation is
2.6 SE. The simulator generates data
consistent with the likelihood it is meant to represent.

## Prior predictive checks

The priors are on the standardised and logit scales described in
[2. Model](02-model.qmd). It is hard to judge from a prior table alone
whether they imply sensible lizards. Instead, we simulate
1000 datasets from the priors and compare them
with what was observed. The aim is not to match the data. It is to
check that the observed data are a plausible outcome under the priors,
and that the priors do not put much weight on biologically absurd
outcomes.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1)
prior_sims <- map(seq_len(n_prior), \(i) {
  params <- draw_params(design, priors, direct_effect = TRUE)
  sim <- simulate_data(params, design)
  list(params = params, sim = sim, latent = attr(sim, "latent"))
})

summarise_sim <- function(dat, latent = NULL) {
  out <- tibble(
    species = factor(species_levels[dat$species], levels = species_levels),
    y2 = dat$y2, y3 = dat$y3, cens = dat$cens, obs_leaf = dat$obs[, "leaf"]
  )
  if (!is.null(latent)) out <- mutate(out, phi = latent$phi, p = latent$p)
  out |>
    group_by(species) |>
    summarise(
      `seen fall 2024` = mean(y2),
      `seen spring 2025` = mean(y3),
      `naive survival (seen either)` = mean(pmax(y2, y3)),
      `leaf below detection limit` = sum(cens) / sum(obs_leaf),
      across(any_of(c("phi", "p")), mean)
    )
}

prior_summary <- map(prior_sims, \(d) summarise_sim(d$sim, d$latent)) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "draw")
observed_summary <- summarise_sim(design)
```
:::


### Resighting and censoring


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
observables <- c("seen fall 2024", "seen spring 2025", "naive survival (seen either)", "leaf below detection limit")

prior_summary |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(observables), names_to = "statistic") |>
  mutate(statistic = factor(statistic, observables)) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, boundary = 0) +
  geom_vline(
    data = observed_summary |>
      pivot_longer(all_of(observables), names_to = "statistic") |>
      mutate(statistic = factor(statistic, observables)),
    aes(xintercept = value), linewidth = 0.7, colour = "#0b0b0b"
  ) +
  facet_grid(species ~ statistic, scales = "free", labeller = labeller(species = species_names)) +
  scale_fill_species(guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Proportion of lizards", y = "Prior draws") +
  theme_lizard() +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(face = "bold.italic"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Prior predictive distributions of observable summaries, per species (histograms), with the observed values (vertical lines). The observed values should fall within the bulk of each distribution.](03-validation_files/figure-html/fig-prior-observables-1.png){#fig-prior-observables width=768}
:::
:::



::: {#tbl-prior-observables .cell tbl-cap='Where the observed values fall in the prior predictive distributions: the percentile of the observed value among prior draws. Values near 0 or 100 would indicate priors in conflict with the data.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
prior_summary |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(observables), names_to = "statistic") |>
  left_join(
    observed_summary |> pivot_longer(all_of(observables), names_to = "statistic", values_to = "observed"),
    by = c("species", "statistic")
  ) |>
  group_by(species, statistic = factor(statistic, observables)) |>
  summarise(observed = first(observed), percentile = 100 * mean(value <= observed), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(observed = round(observed, 3), percentile = round(percentile)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = species, values_from = c(observed, percentile), names_glue = "{species} {.value}") |>
  select(statistic, starts_with("caro"), starts_with("cris"), starts_with("sag")) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

### Survival and detection probabilities

Prior-implied survival and detection are not observable directly, but
their prior distributions show what the model assumes before seeing the
data.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
prior_summary |>
  select(draw, species, `6-month survival (φ)` = phi, `fall detection (p)` = p) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(draw, species), names_to = "quantity") |>
  ggplot(aes(value, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, boundary = 0, alpha = 0.85, position = "identity") +
  facet_grid(species ~ quantity, labeller = labeller(species = species_names)) +
  scale_fill_species(guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Probability", y = "Prior draws") +
  theme_lizard() +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(face = "bold.italic"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Prior distributions of mean 6-month survival probability and fall detection probability per species, averaged over the lizards in the design.](03-validation_files/figure-html/fig-prior-latent-1.png){#fig-prior-latent width=768}
:::
:::


### Performance

Performance is standardised within species, so the observed values have
mean 0 and SD 1 for each trait and species. Simulated performance
should have the same order of magnitude, without being forced to match
exactly.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
perf_sd <- map(prior_sims, \(d) {
  as_tibble(d$latent$u) |>
    mutate(species = factor(species_levels[design$species], levels = species_levels)) |>
    group_by(species) |>
    summarise(across(all_of(perf_traits), sd))
}) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "draw") |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(perf_traits), names_to = "trait") |>
  mutate(trait = factor(trait, perf_traits))

ggplot(perf_sd, aes(value, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, alpha = 0.85, position = "identity") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linewidth = 0.7, colour = "#0b0b0b") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_grid(species ~ trait, labeller = labeller(species = species_names)) +
  scale_fill_species(guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "SD of standardised performance (log scale)", y = "Prior draws") +
  theme_lizard() +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(face = "bold.italic"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Prior predictive SD of each standardised performance trait within species (all lizards, before missingness and censoring). The observed SD is 1 by construction (vertical line). The x-axis is on a log scale.](03-validation_files/figure-html/fig-prior-performance-1.png){#fig-prior-performance width=768}
:::
:::


### Temperature response

The quadratic temperature effect is concave by construction, as near
the optimum of a thermal performance curve. Prior draws show the range
of curves this allows within the observed temperatures.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tb <- lizards |>
  filter(is.na(exclusion), species == "cris", !is.na(tb_sprint)) |>
  pull(tb_sprint)
tb_grid <- seq(min(tb), max(tb), length.out = 101)
w_grid <- (tb_grid - mean(tb)) / sd(tb)
temp_curves <- map(prior_sims[1:100], \(d) {
  tibble(tb = tb_grid, effect = d$params$t[2, 1] * w_grid + d$params$t2[2, 1] * w_grid^2)
}) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "draw")

ggplot(temp_curves, aes(tb, effect, group = draw)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#d9d8d4", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(colour = species_colours[["cris"]], alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Body temperature at trial (°C)", y = "Effect on sprint speed (SD)") +
  theme_lizard()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Effect of body temperature on sprint speed (standardised performance, relative to the species' mean test temperature) for *A. cristatellus*, for 100 prior draws, over the observed range of trial temperatures. Curves can rise, level off or decline, but never curve upwards.](03-validation_files/figure-html/fig-prior-temperature-1.png){#fig-prior-temperature width=768}
:::
:::


### Selection on performance

The priors on $\beta$ and $q$ imply a range of shapes for the
relationship between performance and survival. Curves from individual
prior draws show what kinds of selection the model considers plausible
before seeing the data.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
u_grid <- seq(-2.5, 2.5, length.out = 101)
selection_curves <- map(prior_sims[1:100], \(d) {
  tibble(u = u_grid, phi = plogis(d$params$a[2] + d$params$beta[2, 1] * u + d$params$q[2, 1] * u^2))
}) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "draw")

ggplot(selection_curves, aes(u, phi, group = draw)) +
  geom_line(colour = species_colours[["cris"]], alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Sprint speed (SD from species mean)", y = "6-month survival probability") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_lizard()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Survival probability against sprint speed (standardised, at the species mean of the other traits) for an average female *A. cristatellus*, for 100 prior draws.](03-validation_files/figure-html/fig-prior-selection-1.png){#fig-prior-selection width=768}
:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sel <- map(prior_sims, \(d) {
  phi <- plogis(d$params$a[2] + d$params$beta[2, 1] * seq(-2, 2, 0.1) + d$params$q[2, 1] * seq(-2, 2, 0.1)^2)
  tibble(range = max(phi) - min(phi), beta = d$params$beta[2, 1])
}) |>
  list_rbind()
```
:::


Across sprint speeds from 2 SD below to 2 SD above the mean, the median
prior curve changes survival by 0.3. Survival
changes by more than 0.5 in 21% of
draws, and by more than 0.8 in 2%.
On the odds scale, the central 90% of the prior for the linear term
corresponds to odds of survival changing by a factor of
0.44 to
2.6 per SD of sprint speed.

This is generous. In field studies, linear selection gradients are
typically small, around 0.1--0.2 SD of relative fitness per SD of trait,
and quadratic gradients are smaller still. The priors on $\beta$ and
especially $q$ therefore allow stronger selection than is usually found.
That is conservative in one sense, because the data, not the prior,
must show that selection is weak. But with few survivors in
*A. carolinensis* and *A. sagrei* the prior will carry weight, so
tighter priors on $q$ are worth considering.

### Summary


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pct <- prior_summary |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(observables), names_to = "statistic") |>
  left_join(
    observed_summary |> pivot_longer(all_of(observables), names_to = "statistic", values_to = "observed"),
    by = c("species", "statistic")
  ) |>
  group_by(species, statistic) |>
  summarise(percentile = 100 * mean(value <= first(observed)), .groups = "drop")
sd_q <- quantile(perf_sd$value, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
```
:::


- **Observed resighting and censoring rates are plausible.** All 12
  observed summaries fall between the
  27th and 75th
  percentiles of their prior predictive distributions.
- **Survival and detection.** The priors allow a wide range of 6-month
  survival, concentrated below 0.5, and are nearly uniform for fall
  detection. That is intended: lizards missed in fall but seen in spring
  2025 should inform detection.
- **Performance has the right scale.** The within-species SD of
  simulated performance has a median of 1.26, and 90% of
  draws fall between 0.51 and 2.41,
  against the observed 1.
- **Selection priors are generous**, especially for quadratic selection
  (above). This is the one place where the priors may be revisited
  before calibration.
